## What this chapter does

Use this chapter when setting up a new BNR analytics workstation or moving the environment to a replacement machine.

**Stata is assumed to be installed and licensed.** Do not assume that Git, Python, Quarto, VS Code or the supporting tools are already present.

The repositories and workflow code already exist. A workstation setup therefore has four broad jobs:

1. install the supporting software;
2. obtain the public and authorised private project files;
3. configure the machine-specific paths and Stata startup; and
4. prove that the complete environment works before using it for a live release.

The detailed instructions are kept inside the stage callouts below so that the overall setup pathway remains easy to scan.

## Setup stages

| Stage | Task | Successful result |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | Install the supporting software | Git, Python, Quarto and VS Code are available. |
| **2** | Clone and check the public repository | `info-hub` is available locally and Git recognises it. |
| **3** | Provision the private workspace | The authorised `info-hub-private` data and reference structure is available. |
| **4** | Configure local paths and REDCap access | The public root, private root and required CVD/mortality token-file locations resolve correctly. |
| **5** | Create the Python environment | The project Python packages and PyCap are available. |
| **6** | Configure Stata startup with `profile.do` | Paths, Python, dialogs and the BNR menu load automatically when Stata starts. |
| **7** | Check the Quarto project | Quarto extensions are present and the site renders and previews locally. |
| **8** | Record and verify the workstation setup | Git, private inputs, Stata and Quarto have all been inspected. |

Complete the stages in order on a new machine.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Stage 1: Install the supporting software

Stata is assumed to be installed and licensed. Install the remaining tools only if they are missing.

The links below point to **official landing or Marketplace pages**, rather than version-specific installer files. This makes the manual less likely to become stale when a new software version is released.

### 1. Install VS Code

VS Code is the standard editor used for the BNR repository.

Check first:

```powershell
code --version
```

If it is missing, use the [official VS Code Windows installation page](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/setup/windows).

Alternatively, if WinGet is available:

```powershell
winget install --id Microsoft.VisualStudioCode -e --source winget
```

After installation, close and reopen PowerShell and check:

```powershell
code --version
```

### 2. Install Git

Check:

```powershell
git --version
```

If Git is missing, use the [official Git for Windows installation page](https://git-scm.com/install/windows).

Or install with WinGet:

```powershell
winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget
```

Close and reopen PowerShell, then confirm:

```powershell
git --version
```

VS Code already includes a useful Source Control interface for Git. No additional Git client is required for routine BNR work.

### 3. Install Python 3.13

The current BNR workstation baseline is Python 3.13.

Check:

```powershell
python --version
py --version
```

If Python 3.13 is missing, use the [official Python downloads for Windows](https://www.python.org/downloads/windows/).

Or install the 3.13 series with WinGet:

```powershell
winget install --id Python.Python.3.13 -e --source winget
```

After installation:

```powershell
python --version
python -m pip --version
where.exe python
```

Record the installed Python path. Stage 5 creates the project virtual environment used by BNR.

### 4. Install Quarto

Check:

```powershell
quarto --version
quarto check
```

If Quarto is missing, use the [official Quarto installation page](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/).

Or install with WinGet:

```powershell
winget install --id Posit.Quarto -e --source winget
```

After installation, close and reopen PowerShell and run:

```powershell
quarto --version
quarto check
where.exe quarto
```

### 5. Install TinyTeX

TinyTeX is required when Quarto needs to render PDF outputs.

Check:

```powershell
quarto list tools
```

If TinyTeX is not installed:

```powershell
quarto install tinytex
```

See the [Quarto tool-installation documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/cli/install.html) if installation needs troubleshooting.

### 6. Install the standard VS Code extensions

Install the following small set.

| Extension | Why it is useful |
|---|---|
| [Quarto](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=quarto.quarto) | QMD editing, preview and Quarto authoring support. |
| [Python](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-python.python) | Python environment and code support. |
| [Stata Enhanced](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=kylebarron.stata-enhanced) | Stata syntax colouring, macros, comments and other language-aware highlighting. |
| [Rainbow CSV](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=mechatroner.rainbow-csv) | Makes CSV manifests, QA files and review worklists much easier to inspect by visually separating columns. |
| [GitHub Actions](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=GitHub.vscode-github-actions) | Workflow YAML validation and completion, plus access to workflow runs and logs from VS Code. |
| [YAML](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=redhat.vscode-yaml) | Validation, formatting and completion for the many `.yml` metadata and approval files used by BNR. |

Install them from PowerShell:

```powershell
code --install-extension quarto.quarto
code --install-extension ms-python.python
code --install-extension kylebarron.stata-enhanced
code --install-extension mechatroner.rainbow-csv
code --install-extension GitHub.vscode-github-actions
code --install-extension redhat.vscode-yaml
```

Check:

```powershell
code --list-extensions
```

These are editor aids, not analytical runtime dependencies. A workstation can still run the Stata workflows if an editor extension is temporarily unavailable.

### 7. Browser

Any modern browser can be used for local Quarto review.

The existing BNR edit-session launcher prefers Firefox when it is installed, but Firefox is not required for workstation acceptance.

### Final Stage 1 check

Run:

```powershell
git --version
python --version
quarto --version
code --version
```

Do not continue until each required command returns normally.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Stage 2: Join, clone and check the public repository

The BNR `info-hub` repository is **public by design**. Anyone can read or clone it, but only people given suitable BNR repository permissions can push changes into it.

A team member who will maintain the site therefore needs both:

- a GitHub account; and
- BNR write access to `UWI-BNR/info-hub`.

### 1. Obtain BNR GitHub access

If the user does not already have a GitHub account, create one at the official GitHub website.

Give the GitHub username to the BNR team lead. The team lead decides who should be authorised to maintain the repository; a BNR GitHub repository or organisation administrator then grants the required access.

For routine maintainers, **Write** access is normally sufficient.

Accept the GitHub invitation if one is sent.

Public users who have not been granted write access can still view, clone, fork and propose changes. They cannot push directly to the BNR repository.

### 2. Sign in to GitHub from VS Code

Open VS Code.

Use the **Accounts** menu and choose **Sign in with GitHub**. Complete the browser sign-in if prompted.

This allows VS Code to authenticate later when the user pushes an authorised branch.

### 3. Clone `info-hub` using VS Code

In VS Code:

1. Open **Source Control**.
2. Choose **Clone Repository**.
3. Select **Clone from GitHub** or paste:

```text
https://github.com/UWI-BNR/info-hub.git
```

4. Choose the local parent folder where the repository should be stored.
5. Open the cloned repository when VS Code offers to do so.

### 4. Check Git identity

Open **Terminal > New Terminal** in VS Code and run:

```powershell
git config user.name
git config user.email
```

If either is blank, configure it using the user's normal professional Git identity:

```powershell
git config --global user.name "Full name"
git config --global user.email "name@example.org"
```

### 5. Check the repository

In the VS Code terminal:

```powershell
git status
git remote -v
```

The remote should point to the UWI-BNR `info-hub` repository.

The branch name is shown in the lower-left VS Code status bar.

### 6. Create local setup notes

At the repository root:

```powershell
New-Item local-setup-notes.md
```

`local-setup-notes.md` is machine-specific and should remain outside version control.

A short template is provided in Stage 8.

### Public repository rule

Because `info-hub` is public, **never commit confidential data, credentials, REDCap tokens, private review files or private staging material**.

Those belong in the private companion environment described in Stage 3.

### Final Stage 2 check

Confirm:

- the repository opens normally in VS Code;
- the intended user is signed in to GitHub;
- `git status` recognises the repository;
- the remote points to `UWI-BNR/info-hub`; and
- `local-setup-notes.md` is not staged for Git.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Command-line clone alternative

A user who prefers the terminal can clone the same public repository with:

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/UWI-BNR/info-hub.git
cd info-hub
```

The VS Code route above is the normal BNR team method.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Stage 3: Provision the private companion workspace

The public repository is not enough to run the BNR analytical workflows.

The workstation also needs an authorised private companion root, later assigned to:

`$BNR_PRIVATE`

The private root contains or receives:

```text
data/
  raw/
  frozen/
  derived/

outputs/
  staging/

logs/
  private/

work/
```

Provision or restore this workspace using the organisation's approved secure-storage process.

Do **not** copy private registry data from an informal or unapproved source simply to make the workstation run.

### Required retained inputs

Check that the authorised private workspace includes the current retained inputs needed by the workflows, including where applicable:

- the frozen historical CVD dataset under `$BNR_DATA_FROZEN`;
- Barbados population reference data under `$BNR_PRIVATE_WORK`;
- the WHO standard-population reference under `$BNR_PRIVATE_WORK`; and
- any other controlled reference files required by the current analytical code.

The exact machine path is configured in Stage 4.

See [The BNR analytics and publishing environment](environment.qmd) for the purpose of each private location.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Stage 4: Configure local paths and REDCap access

The public repository contains a path template:

`scripts/stata/config/bnr_paths_TEMPLATE.do`

Copy it:

```powershell
Copy-Item `
  scripts/stata/config/bnr_paths_TEMPLATE.do `
  scripts/stata/config/bnr_paths_LOCAL.do
```

Open the local copy:

```powershell
code scripts/stata/config/bnr_paths_LOCAL.do
```

### 1. Set the two roots

Edit:

```stata
global BNR_REPO    "C:/your/path/info-hub"
global BNR_PRIVATE "C:/your/secure/path/info-hub-private"
```

Also set the paths—not the values—of the REDCap tokens used by the authorised workflows:

```stata
global BNR_REDCAP_TOKEN_FILE      "C:/your/secure/path/bnr_redcap_token.txt"
global BNR_MORT_REDCAP_TOKEN_FILE "C:/your/secure/path/bnr_mort_redcap_token.txt"
```

The mortality token setting is required by Mortality Step 1. If the current tracked path template does not yet contain that line, add it to the local file and update the tracked template through the normal code-change process before handover.

The remaining standard globals are derived automatically, including:

- `$BNR_STATA`
- `$BNR_DATA_RAW`
- `$BNR_DATA_FROZEN`
- `$BNR_DATA_DERIVED`
- `$BNR_STAGING`
- `$BNR_PRIVATE_WORK`
- `$BNR_PRIVATE_LOGS`
- `$BNR_PUBLIC`
- `$BNR_SITE`

### 2. Configure the REDCap token files

Each token text file must:

- be stored outside the public repository;
- contain only the API token on one line; and
- be accessible only to authorised users.

Do not put the token itself in `bnr_paths_LOCAL.do`, another DO file, a log, Git or this manual.

### 3. Test the configuration

In Stata:

```stata
do "scripts/stata/config/bnr_paths_LOCAL.do"
```

Then:

```stata
display "$BNR_REPO"
display "$BNR_PRIVATE"
display "$BNR_DATA_RAW"
display "$BNR_DATA_DERIVED"
display "$BNR_STAGING"
display "$BNR_PUBLIC"
display "$BNR_SITE"
```

Loading the configuration now stops with an error if the repository root is
wrong, a required private folder is absent, or the private workspace/token path
sits inside the public Git repository.

Check the token files exist without displaying their contents:

```stata
confirm file "$BNR_REDCAP_TOKEN_FILE"
confirm file "$BNR_MORT_REDCAP_TOKEN_FILE"
```

### Important

`bnr_paths_LOCAL.do` is workstation-specific. It must **not** be committed to Git.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Stage 5: Create the Python environment

The repository uses a local Python virtual environment called:

`venv-info-hub`

Using a project environment keeps BNR support packages separate from unrelated Python work.

### 1. Create the environment

From the repository root:

```powershell
python -m venv venv-info-hub
```

Confirm it exists:

```powershell
dir venv-info-hub
```

### 2. Activate it

```powershell
.\venv-info-hub\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

The prompt should begin with:

```text
(venv-info-hub)
```

If PowerShell blocks activation, use the smallest practical policy change for the current user:

```powershell
Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser
```

Then activate the environment again.

### 3. Install the project packages

With the virtual environment active:

```powershell
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

This installs the supported analyst/notebook packages and **PyCap**, which the
REDCap extraction imports as `redcap`.

### 4. Check the environment

From the repository root, run the tracked environment check:

```powershell
python scripts/python/check-python-environment.py
```

It must report Python 3.13, list every required package and finish with
`PASSED`. It does not connect to REDCap or read private data.

Then:

```powershell
where.exe python
```

The first Python path should point inside:

`venv-info-hub\Scripts\python.exe`

### 5. Record the environment

Record the Python version and environment path in `local-setup-notes.md`.

The two requirement files have different purposes:

- `requirements.txt` is the maintained list of direct project packages and
  compatible version ranges. Use it for routine workstation setup and CI.
- `requirements-freeze.txt` records the exact full Windows/Python 3.13
  environment that was tested at handover, including indirect dependencies.
  Use it to compare or reproduce a known environment when troubleshooting; it
  is not the routine cross-platform installation file.

After an authorised dependency change has been installed and tested on the
canonical BNR Windows workstation, refresh the frozen record from the repository
root:

```powershell
python -m pip freeze --all | Set-Content -Encoding utf8 requirements-freeze.txt
```

Review and commit changes to both requirement files together.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Stage 6: Configure Stata startup with `profile.do`

Stata is assumed to be installed. The workstation still needs the BNR project configuration to load automatically at startup.

The current BNR `profile.do` performs four jobs:

1. adds the BNR ado and dialog directories;
2. loads `bnr_paths_LOCAL.do`;
3. builds the **User > BNR** menu; and
4. tells Stata which Python executable to use.

### 1. Find the personal Stata directory

In Stata:

```stata
sysdir
```

Identify the `PERSONAL` directory.

Place or edit:

`profile.do`

in that personal directory so Stata runs it automatically at startup.

### 2. Use the BNR profile pattern

The current workstation profile follows this pattern:

```stata
* BNR INFO-HUB ADO AND DIALOG DIRECTORIES
capture adopath + "C:/your/path/info-hub/scripts/stata/ado"
capture noisily adopath + "C:/your/path/info-hub/scripts/stata/dialogs"

* Load BNR workstation configuration
do "C:/your/path/info-hub/scripts/stata/config/bnr_paths_LOCAL.do"

* Build the BNR menu
do "$BNR_STATA/menu/bnr_menu.do"

* Python
python set exec ///
    "C:/your/path/info-hub/venv-info-hub/Scripts/python.exe", permanently
noisily python query
```

The machine-specific parts are the repository path and Python executable.

This is based on the active BNR workstation `profile.do`; do not copy another user's absolute paths unchanged.

### 3. Restart Stata

Close and reopen Stata.

Confirm the startup sequence completes without an error.

Check:

```stata
python query
```

The Python executable should be the one configured in `profile.do`.

### 4. Check Python from inside Stata

```stata
python:
from redcap import Project
print("BNR Python / PyCap check passed")
end
```

### 5. Check the menu

Confirm:

**User > BNR**

is visible and contains:

- **Update CVD dashboard**
- **Update mortality dashboard**
- **Produce briefing**
- **Produce tables**

The menu should now load automatically whenever Stata starts.

### Why `profile.do` matters

Routine analysts should not need to remember a sequence of setup commands before running a workflow.

Loading paths, dialogs, the BNR menu and Python at Stata startup makes the workstation state predictable and reduces reliance on hard-coded fallback paths inside individual DO files.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Stage 7: Check the Quarto project

### 1. Check the committed Quarto extension

The site currently includes the Font Awesome extension inside the repository:

`site/_extensions/quarto-ext/fontawesome/`

After cloning, check that the folder exists:

```powershell
dir site\_extensions\quarto-ext\fontawesome
```

A normal workstation should **not** need to reinstall this extension because it is part of the committed site source.

### 2. Activate the Python environment

From the repository root:

```powershell
.\venv-info-hub\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

The site has a Python pre-render step, so use the project environment when rendering locally.

### 3. Render the site

```powershell
cd site
quarto check
quarto render
```

A successful render creates or refreshes:

`site/_site/`

### 4. Test preview

```powershell
quarto preview --host 127.0.0.1 --port 4200
```

Open the local site in a browser.

Inspect several pages, including:

- the Technical Manual;
- a dashboard;
- the tabulations page; and
- a briefing page.

Confirm the navigation, tables, Mermaid diagrams and downloads render normally.

Stop preview with:

```text
Ctrl + C
```

### 5. Test the standard edit-session launcher

The repository includes:

`start-info-hub-edit.bat`

This is the normal convenience tool for starting a local Info-Hub editing session.

Double-click the BAT file from the repository root.

It should:

- open the repository in VS Code;
- activate `venv-info-hub` for the Quarto preview process;
- start the preview server on port 4200; and
- open the local Info-Hub in a browser.

The launcher works out the repository path from its own location, so it should not need machine-specific editing.

Keep the preview Command Prompt open while using the local site. Close it, or press `Ctrl + C`, to stop the preview server.

If the launcher fails, use the manual preview commands above and investigate the message shown by the launcher. Chapter 10 describes normal daily use.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Stage 8: Record and verify the workstation setup

Finish with a human inspection of the complete environment.

### 1. Public repository

From the repository root:

```powershell
git status
```

Confirm:

- Git recognises the repository;
- the intended branch is checked out;
- `bnr_paths_LOCAL.do` is not staged;
- `venv-info-hub/` is not staged;
- `local-setup-notes.md` is not staged; and
- there are no unexplained changes.

### 2. Private workspace

In Stata:

```stata
display "$BNR_PRIVATE"
display "$BNR_DATA_FROZEN"
display "$BNR_DATA_DERIVED"
display "$BNR_STAGING"
display "$BNR_PRIVATE_WORK"
display "$BNR_PRIVATE_LOGS"
```

Go to the folders and confirm the required retained private/reference files actually exist.

### 3. REDCap configuration

Run:

```stata
confirm file "$BNR_REDCAP_TOKEN_FILE"
confirm file "$BNR_MORT_REDCAP_TOKEN_FILE"
```

Do not print the token.

A live REDCap extract is not required merely to prove that the workstation has been configured.

### 4. Stata startup

Restart Stata one final time.

Confirm:

- `profile.do` runs without error;
- `python query` points to the intended Python;
- PyCap imports successfully; and
- **User > BNR** is available without manually loading any setup file.

### 5. Quarto

With `venv-info-hub` active:

```powershell
cd site
quarto render
```

Open the rendered Technical Manual and confirm the site behaves normally.

### 6. Record the setup

Maintain a short local file:

`local-setup-notes.md`

For example:

```markdown
# Local setup notes

Machine:
User:
Setup date:

Public repo path:
Private root path:
CVD REDCap token-file location:
Mortality REDCap token-file location:

Stata version:
Python version:
Python environment:
Python executable used by Stata:
Quarto version:
Git version:
VS Code version:
TinyTeX check:

BNR menu startup check:
Quarto render check:
Private reference-data check:

Setup issues / local decisions:
```

Record the token **file location**, never the token itself.
:::

## Moving to another workstation

Treat a replacement machine as a new setup rather than copying random configuration fragments from the old one.

Portable:

- the Git repository;
- committed Quarto extensions; and
- approved project source files.

Machine-specific:

- `bnr_paths_LOCAL.do`;
- `profile.do`;
- `venv-info-hub/`;
- the REDCap token files;
- `local-setup-notes.md`; and
- the authorised private workspace.

Recreate the machine-specific pieces deliberately, then repeat Stage 8 before using the workstation for a live analytical release.
